TUCSON, Ariz. (13 News) - In less than two months, six different incidents have been reported involving a student bringing a weapon to school in Pima County.
Those incidents happened between Aug. 10 and Sept. 16 and involved seven students. Of those seven, six allegedly brought a firearm to school.

The incidents happened at Gallego Intermediate, Alice Vail Middle, Marana High, Sunnyside High, Tortolita Middle and Pueblo High. That means the Marana, Tucson, and Sunnyside unified school districts were involved.
James Horton, a public information officer from the Tucson Police Department, said the TPD recognizes the seriousness of any incident involving a weapon at a school.
“We recognize the seriousness of any time a weapon goes onto a school campus; it’s very serious. But it’s statistically very low,” Horton said.
Horton said it is difficult to say whether the number of incidents is more than usual because different law enforcement agencies have responded to the incidents depending on location
“I don’t have hard stats in front of me, but you tell me that you’ve had six incidents – that’s concerning to me,” Mike Kurtenbach, the Arizona Department of Education’s school safety director, said.
Kurtenbach said this comes after the department added more than 400 school resource officers to schools across the state since 2018.
“They start to hear what’s going on; they become that trusted adult that’s on the campus,” Kurtenbach said.
Kurtenbach said he hopes the high number of incidents does not necessarily correlate with an actual increase in weapons getting onto campus.
“If we have an officer on that’s on the campus, yeah, that affords us the opportunity to catch that incident – a gun, a knife – whatever that case may be,” Kurtenbach said.
Horton said he agrees and thinks it could be the case, especially as TPD has begun emphasizing its “see something say something” outlook.

“We’re seeing that more students are not afraid to speak up if they see a student with a weapon so that they can alert staff and so that the staff can promptly and appropriately handle the situation,” he said.
Horton said he wants parents to know that regardless of whether a school has an officer, schools do have an emergency plan.

“Whether an officer is staffed at the time or not, generally it’s a lights-and-sirens response, numerous patrol officers responding to get into that school quickly and safely to make the school as safe as possible,” Horton said.

Kurtenbach said that after seeing the data and seeing how many schools and districts have requested more school resource officers, he has created a decision package to go to the governor’s desk to grow the school resource officer program.
### **BREAKDOWN OF INCIDENTS**

### Article Summary

-   ALPINA designed the V8 in the E53 X5 4.6is, yet never got to sell an ALPINA X5 of its own.
-   A 500 PS supercharged E70 ALPINA X5 would have filled the 200 PS gap between the X5 4.8i and the X5 M. .
-   Priced below the XB7, an ALPINA X5 would likely have outsold the XB7, B6 Gran Coupe, and B8 Gran Coupe in the US.

In 2001, BMW wanted a faster X5 and didn’t have one, so it borrowed ALPINA’s. The 4.6-liter V8 in the [E53 X5 4.6is](https://www.bmwblog.com/2023/03/10/driving-a-2003-bmw-x5-4-6is/) started life as the engine ALPINA developed for the [E39 B10 V8](https://www.bmwblog.com/2017/01/31/20-years-bmw-e39-alpina-b10-v8-anniversary-buchloe/), and BMW put it into production as the M62B46. ALPINA did the engineering and BMW sold the SUV. Nobody thought to put the ALPINA badge on it, and 25 years later that still annoys me. Of all the ALPINAs that never got built, the X5 is the one I’d bring back if I could only pick one. It isn’t the most exotic idea on the list. It’s the most obvious one, which somehow makes it worse.
## Buchloe Tried Weirder Things Than This

Nobody has shown an ALPINA X5 prototype in public, and I haven’t found evidence that one existed. I wouldn’t bet much against it, though. This is the company that pulled the three-cylinder out of an i8, reworked the rear subframe, and [fitted the 2.0-liter four-cylinder](https://www.bmwblog.com/2025/10/01/alpina-i8-photos/) from the M135i, for somewhere around 460 hp combined. Keeping it alive took two extra intercoolers ahead of the front wheels and a different eight-speed automatic. ALPINA finished one prototype before the cost of recalibrating the software and crash-testing the car ended the project. I [covered that story in 2020](https://www.bmwblog.com/2020/11/22/how-alpina-bmw-i8-almost-happened/), and I still think about that car more than I should.

Then there’s the MINI. In the early 2000s, [ALPINA built an R53 Cooper S called the “Lux,”](https://www.bmwblog.com/2025/09/27/mini-by-alpina-rare-appearance/) with dark blue trim outside and Alcantara on nearly every surface inside. It would have cost too much to sell, so ALPINA dropped it and moved on to the E63 6 Series. Both cars turned up at ALPINA’s 60th anniversary gathering at the Penzing air base last year.
A company willing to build a luxury MINI and a four-cylinder i8 almost certainly sketched an X5 at some point. If nobody in Buchloe did, somebody in Munich should have asked.
## The XB7 Is Great, And It’s Still The Wrong ALPINA

[![BMW ALPINA XB7 2026 US EDITION 07](https://cdn.bmwblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/bmw-alpina-xb7-2026-us-edition-07-830x553.jpg "BMW ALPINA XB7 2026 US EDITION 07")](https://cdn.bmwblog.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/03/bmw-alpina-xb7-2026-us-edition-07.jpg)

I have a soft spot for the XB7. The cabin is as nice as anything BMW sells, and it drives with a calm the regular X7 never quite finds. BMW never built an X7 M, so a three-row V8 flagship with 631 hp (612 hp at launch) was an easy call for America. I get why it exists. But the XB7 started north of $150,000, or [even more for a special edition](https://www.bmwblog.com/2026/03/09/2026-alpina-xb7-walkaround-video/), and most people shopping at that level don’t need a third row. They need an X5. It was BMW’s first SUV, and it’s still the one people actually buy, so an ALPINA version would have cost less and reached far more buyers.
